newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean fishermen vow to boycott Japanese goods.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean fishermen vow to boycott Japanese goods.

text.p: More than 1,000 South Korean fishermen, workers and civic leaders vowed on Monday to launch a campaign to boycott Japanese goods in protest at Japan's seizure of South Korean fishing boats in disputed waters.

Witnesses said more than 1,000 fishermen and representatives of civic groups staged a noisy demonstration at a Seoul park, while riot police briefly clashed with about 400 supporting union workers trying to march on the Japanese embassy.
They denounced Japan for capturing five fishing boats in the past several weeks in waters recently claimed by Japan. No serious injuries were reported.
The protesters, demanding an apology for the seizure, asked Tokyo to withdraw its unilateral announcement in January to expand its territorial waters, witnesses said.
The protesters, wearing headbands and sashes across their shoulders, shouted slogans such as "All citizens, rise against Japan", "Japan kneel down and apologise" and "Crush Japanese atrocities".
Dozens of protest leaders were allowed to march to the embassy and deliver letters of protest.

Japan, which in January expanded its territorial waters in accordance with a new maritime convention introduced by the United Nations in November 1994, has released all of the five boats and their crew except for the captains of two vessels.
South Korea has agreed to revise a 1965 fisheries agreement but insists the existing pact be respected until a revision is drawn up.
Han Hong-chol, a released sailor, told the protesters at the Seoul park that he and his colleagues were badly beaten by Japanese investigators.

Last week, South Korea's Vice Foreign Minister Lee Ki-choo called in the Japanese ambassador to Seoul, Shintaro Yamashita, to lodge a formal protest over the seizures and to demand steps to ensure such an incident is not repeated.

Japan and South Korea have maintained uneasy relations since Japan colonised the Korean peninsula between 1910 and 1945. Tensions have frequently risen between Japan and South Korea over territorial claims.
Both countries claim sovereignty over barren outcrops of rock in the Sea of Japan midway between Japan and South Korea. The islands are called Tokdo in South Korea and Takeshima in Japan.
